title: Keep plan-forbidden properties out of emit calls

facts.note: Bun realization; source files of the Bun codebase.

Requires an AST observer that finds every emit-like call (existing or changed) whose first argument is a concrete id held by the tracking-plan registry, reads the properties object on the same statement, and re-evaluates all such calls when a plan item's forbidden_properties list or a call's named item id changes. Not limited to edited calls.
Validator finding from bun_telemetry_code after comparing normalized top-level keys against the item's forbidden_properties list.
Rule is inert until the repository has adopted the telemetry tracking plan (family-wide adoption gate).

fires: After adoption, any emit-like call names a declared tracking-plan item and its properties object has a top-level key in that item's forbidden_properties list (e.g. a raw payload, secret or prompt).
The plan forbids a snake_case name and the code writes the same name in camelCase as a top-level key of the properties object.
A plan change adds a name to an item's forbidden_properties list that an existing, unchanged emit call already passes.
A call's named item id is changed to an item whose forbidden list contains one of the call's existing keys.
doesNotFire: The emit-like call's first argument is an id the registry does not hold (that is the raw-string rule's finding).
The properties object carries a key the plan merely does not declare (undeclared-key drift belongs to the generated contract).
The value is passed via a shorthand property, which carries no name of its own and is invisible to this scan.
A matching name appears only inside a nested object (nested objects are judged at their own level, not as top-level keys of this call).
The repository has not yet adopted the tracking plan.

given: After adoption, an emit-like call (a telemetry emit whose first argument is a declared concrete tracking-plan item id) with a properties object literal following that argument on the same statement.
when: The call exists or changes, or the named item's forbidden_properties list or the call's item id changes.
then: No top-level named key of the properties object MAY match a property the plan forbids on that item, compared after stripping separators and folding case (shorthand properties carry no name and are not scanned; nested objects are judged at their own level).
prefer: Pass the identifier, not the thing it identifies, and leave out any property the named item's plan forbids.
avoid: Attaching raw payloads, secrets or prompts the plan forbids on the named item.
Evading the check by renaming case/separators (snake_case vs camelCase) instead of removing the property.
Treating properties the plan merely does not declare as forbidden or removing them for this rule; undeclared-key drift is the generated contract's concern.
unless: The call names an id the registry does not hold: that is the raw-string rule's finding; double-reporting here would be noise.
Inert until adoption, like every rule in this family.
why: The forbidden list is a privacy and cost promise, so it is enforced where data leaves: the emit call itself, against the plan entry the call names.
evidence: bun_telemetry_code validator reports no forbidden-property finding for emit-like calls naming declared items.
For every emit call naming a declared item (not only changed ones), every normalized top-level key of the properties object is absent from that item's forbidden_properties list.
verifier_detail: Scope: only emit-like calls whose first argument is a declared concrete id in the tracking-plan registry; undeclared ids are skipped (raw-string rule reports them). All qualifying calls are checked after adoption, regardless of whether the call itself changed.
properties_object: the object literal following the first argument of the emit-like call, on the same statement.
forbidden_property: a name in the item's forbidden_properties list (raw payloads, secrets, prompts): what must never leave the process on that item.
Normalization: every top-level key has separators stripped and case folded before comparison against the item's forbidden list; the plan writes snake_case, code may write camelCase.
Shorthand properties carry no name of their own and are invisible to this scan; nested objects are judged at their own level.
Properties the plan merely does not declare are not forbidden; undeclared-key drift is the generated contract's concern, not this rule's.
audit: Source name: Forbidden properties never reach an emit call
Depends on planner.telemetry.tracking-plan-schema (forbidden-property list comes from the tracking-plan item).
